title: Farzi Café, Rishtedar, and the New Wave of Indian Restaurant Brands Landing in America
excerpt: From Bellevue to Miami, India's most ambitious restaurateurs are betting that the US is finally ready for Indian food that goes beyond the buffet.
body:
Something remarkable is happening in the American dining landscape. In the space of a few weeks, Farzi Café opened its first US location in Bellevue, Washington. Rishtedar, an Indian fine-dining concept from Santiago, Chile, debuted in Miami's Wynwood neighborhood. And Sanjeev Kapoor's Yellow Chilli confirmed a Santa Clara, California opening for next summer. These are not isolated openings — they are the leading edge of a wave.

## Farzi Café: Molecular Gastronomy Meets Masala

Zorawar Kalra, the man behind Farzi Café and the son of the legendary Jiggs Kalra — known as the "czar of Indian cuisine" — has a stated mission: to make Indian food mainstream in America. His Bellevue location, nestled inside the upscale Bellevue Square, is the beachhead.

The menu is designed to surprise. Think achari chicken tacos, karela calamari, Parle-G cheesecake, and mango puchka tartlets — dishes that take familiar Indian flavors and present them through techniques borrowed from molecular gastronomy and global fusion. The London outpost already carries a Michelin Guide listing. Now Kalra, who oversees more than two dozen restaurants across 11 countries through his Massive Restaurants group, is planning a coast-to-coast US expansion.

"One of the biggest challenges I face is retaining top talent," Kalra told reporters, noting that he flew in his core team from New Delhi and London for the opening, including Chef Gaurav Chawla and global beverage R&D head Engjell Shala.

## Rishtedar: A Chilean Detour to Miami

Meanwhile, 3,000 miles to the southeast, Rishtedar has taken a more unconventional path to America. Founded in Santiago, Chile, by Vikram Thadani — who was born to Indian parents in Chile — the fine-dining concept started as an import business before becoming one of Santiago's most talked-about restaurants.

"Creating an experience that captures my heritage and can serve as an introduction to Indian culture was our aim," Thadani said. "Rishtedar means 'family,' and as soon as our diners step foot in here, we like to expose them to many traditions."

The Wynwood location, designed by Mico Design & Co., features bright colors and textures reflecting Indian culture. The menu runs from sesame-breaded shrimp with 12 spices to lamb marinated in masala, with dishes arriving on blazing charcoal for tableside smokiness.

## The Bigger Picture

These openings are part of a broader pattern that Restaurant Business Online recently called "the year of redefining Indian food in America." London's Dishoom, valued at nearly $400 million after an L Catterton investment, is preparing a New York City debut. Michelin-starred Indienne has expanded from Chicago to Hudson Yards. JKS Restaurants has signed a 15-year lease in Manhattan's NoMAD district. Curry Up Now, the Indian fast-casual chain, just received venture capital from a fund co-led by Joe Montana.

Even Wonder, the fast-growing food-hall and delivery venture, has launched Dabba — an Indian concept named after Mumbai's legendary dabbawallas — now testing in four Philadelphia locations with plans for a nationwide rollout.

## What NRIs Should Know

For Indian Americans, the wave brings both pride and a twinge of irony. Many grew up watching their parents' home cooking get reduced to "curry" by American classmates. Now, Indian food is one of the hottest categories in US dining — complete with celebrity chefs, private-equity backing, and molecular gastronomy.

The question is whether these concepts can maintain authenticity while scaling. Wonder's Dabba and Curry Up Now's Biryani Burrito represent the fast-casual end; Farzi and Rishtedar sit at the premium tier. Together, they are building the infrastructure for Indian cuisine to occupy every price point in the American market — something Chinese, Japanese, and Mexican food achieved decades ago.

## What's Next

Watch for Sanjeev Kapoor's Yellow Chilli in Santa Clara next summer, Dishoom's New York opening later this year, and JKS Restaurants' NoMAD debut within 12 to 15 months. If even half these concepts succeed, 2026 may be remembered as the year Indian food finally went from ethnic niche to American mainstream.
author: Diaspora Desk
